coverage.method: Complete page-by-page extracted text read; rendered pages separately listed where inspected.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: British visitors found ruined infrastructure, secularized/abandoned buildings, altered political symbols and revived fashionable Paris. These observations distinguish temporary disruption from permanent change and disprove some visitors’ expectations of universal savagery.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: British travellers; Fanny Burney; Paris1802; revolutionary ruins; tourism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Attribute observations and expectations; do not treat a traveller sample as a complete national survey.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Doyle gives intellectual development and public confidence central roles, while stressing that neither collapse nor revolutionary careers were planned. Cahiers broadened regeneration beyond the educated elite. Enlightenment supplied both rational reform and intolerance of opponents.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Enlightenment; public opinion; revolutionary origins; national regeneration; unintended consequences
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve author’s weighting without denying social/economic conditions or inventing a planned Enlightenment conspiracy.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Departments, metric/decimal measures and Civil Code were enduring rational reforms. Guillotine humanitarian design diverged from terroristic use. Resistance and revolutionaries’ refusal to recognize good-faith opposition made coercion escalate.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: administrative rationalization; metric system; Civil Code; guillotine; resistance and violence
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not reduce violence to either original benevolent intent or an inevitable single doctrine; author recognizes intimidation from1789.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Nobility: constructed antagonism and unequal losses
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Society of Thirty mobilized anti-noble opinion despite reform willingness in noble cahiers. Loss of office, precedence, feudal income and legal recognition did not erase noble identity or all wealth; landed recovery coexisted with trauma and lost monopoly.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: nobility; Society of Thirty; aristocracy; venality; émigré property; noble survival
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep material, corporate, political and psychological losses distinct; not total dispossession or unchanged status.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Initially cooperative clergy lost revenues, corporate autonomy, monasteries and benefices; monks and nuns responded differently. Refractory and constitutional clergy experienced successive distinct persecutions. Concordat did not restore old Gallican institutions.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: clergy losses; monasticism; nuns; clerical oath; schism; constitutional clergy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve group and stage distinctions, and source’s specific little-church attribution as written without outside correction.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Antonelli’s anguished criticism coexisted with support for Concordat. Papal martyrdom and lay loyalty to nonjurors increased Roman authority despite material losses; the restored clergy focused on pastoral work. Mutual Church-republican hostility persisted to1905.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: papacy; Antonelli; ultramontane authority; Church-State separation; anti-republican Catholicism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish quoted dread from final judgment, material loss from spiritual gain, and historical Catholic conspiracy accusations from Doyle’s endorsement.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Education: reform projects and institutional collapse
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Rational schemes including Condorcet’s failed to replace lost funding, teachers and institutions. Departmental central schools and higher schools left primary education underfunded; attendance and literacy declined before later reconstruction.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: education; Condorcet plan; central schools; Oratorians; university abolition; literacy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Require routes for provisions, failures and measurements; do not equate declarations of educational rights with provision.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Grand welfare legislation and Great Book of National Benevolence lacked wartime resources. Church, municipal, endowed and voluntary income collapsed; nursing orders were suppressed. Partial Directory/Napoleonic recovery did not restore former scale, harming poor and sick over generations.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: poor relief; mendicity; Great Book; hospitals; charitable orders; nationalization of hospital lands
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve institutional mechanisms and chronology; no inference that national welfare was actually funded and delivered.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Economic crisis and social repercussions of reform
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Harvest failure and subsistence expectations shaped1789; sansculottes constrained liberal policy. Landlords’ rent increases and tithe substitution offset relief for tenants, while aristocratic/clerical institutional loss destroyed services, luxury employment and urban demand.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: subsistence; moral economy; rents; tithe abolition; luxury trades; servants; urban decline
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish owners from tenants and initial harvest shock from later legislative effects.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Land-backed confidence, refusal to reduce debt and inadequate tax collection encouraged overissue; war entrenched it. Inflation benefited debtors and national-land buyers, hurt creditors/wage earners and undermined business, employment and charity.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: assignats; overissue; national lands; debtors/creditors; wage erosion; unemployment
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Maintain causal hierarchy and qualified counterfactual about proper withdrawal; figures concern nominal versus real value.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Trade collapse, continental reorientation and uneven industry
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Slave revolt, British war, blockade and French embargoes wrecked colonial commerce. Continental markets and protection aided war industries, Belgian production and cotton, while silk and trade recovery took decades. Structural opportunity did not mean general prosperity.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: overseas trade; blockade; Saint-Domingue trade; continental markets; cotton; silk; war industries
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Separate permanent reorientation from eventual volume recovery and compare sectors rather than totalizing collapse.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Investment and agriculture: continuity despite reform
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Abolished barriers and guilds created preconditions without automatic enterprise. Land sales and loss of venal investment reinforced conservative portfolios; rents, taxes, inheritance, livestock drain and conscription limited farm change despite more mouths fed.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: investment habits; national land purchases; agricultural productivity; inheritance; sharecropping; potatoes
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Avoid bourgeois-capitalist transformation assumptions; preserve limited improvement and continuity.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Most ordinary people faced insecurity and intrusive state power. Popular resistance often sought autonomy rather than restoration. Worker/peasant émigrés, terror victims and draft evasion broaden the picture. Sansculotte moral economy and local democracy also conflicted with elite liberalism.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: anti-revolution; popular resistance; conscription evasion; banditry; moral economy; sansculottes
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not reserve popular politics for sansculottes, or equate every oppositional slogan with a fully counter-revolutionary programme.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Landowners, national land sales and Notables
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Property owners were clear beneficiaries; bourgeois purchases outweighed the limited increase in peasant ownership share, while nobles retained large estates. Security fears favoured dictatorship and later restoration respected the land settlement.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: landowners; bourgeois gains; peasant proprietors; Notables; national lands; property security
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve distribution, share versus number, and mechanism linking property guarantees to political support.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Venal-office compensation was inadequate and deregulation invited unqualified practice before Napoleonic licensing. Administrative expansion reversed anti-intendant ideals, creating stable careers, qualifications and pensions for bourgeois entrants.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: professions; venal-office compensation; licensing; bureaucracy; careers open to talent; pensions
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish initial losses and later gains; not unbroken professional liberalization.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Military careers, revolutionary commitment and costs
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Officer emigration accelerated promotion from ranks; army expansion gave opportunity and plunder but imposed heavy deaths and unwilling service. Soldiers became political guardians and privileged members of imperial society.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: military careers; officer corps; careers open to talent; army politics; war casualties
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep benefit and mortality/conscription qualifications; ideological commitment was substantive, not merely material gain.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Civil equality improved Protestant status beyond1787 but provoked southern antagonism; Terror/dechristianization and public-worship restrictions also harmed Protestants. Consular salaried churches secured status while weakening democratic traditions.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Protestants; civil equality; Cévennes; Gard; Protestant churches; religious toleration
findings.eventual_draft_checks: No smooth uninterrupted liberation narrative or inference that Protestant support exempted them from persecution.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Reform preceded1789, but citizenship reached assimilated Jews before Alsatian Ashkenazim. Religious persecution and popular prejudice survived formal equality; later state control sought civic consolidation without returning to old marginal status.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Jews; Grégoire; Alsatian Jews; Ashkenazim; emancipation1790/1791; antisemitism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve phases, groups and distinction between civil status and social/religious safety.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Slavery abolition: initiative, race and wartime expediency
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Abolitionist weakness, colonial representation and free-coloured rights preceded slave rebellion. Sonthonax’s local concessions and1793 emancipation were unauthorized responses to military/social crisis; Convention ratification in1794 also served war aims.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: slavery; Amis des Noirs; Ogé; free people of colour; Sonthonax; abolition1794
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish free-coloured citizenship from enslaved freedom; restore agency of rebellion and commissioners rather than only metropolitan legislation.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Toussaint, restored slavery and Haitian independence
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Toussaint shifted from Spain to France after abolition, while black militarization included persecution of coloureds. British disease losses and later French expedition shaped outcomes; restored slavery did not return to Saint-Domingue, which became Haiti.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Toussaint Louverture; Saint-Domingue; Haiti; slavery restoration; Dessalines
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve changing alliances, racial distinctions and Haiti exception; independence follows resistance, not a French grant.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Revolution/Napoleon erased or transformed states, secularized Germany and shifted territory. Most French territorial gains disappeared after1815 while rivals benefited. Dutch decline and France’s setback reinforced already emerging British economic leadership.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: European territorial change; German secularization; Holy Roman Empire; British ascendancy; post1815 settlement
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Separate revolutionary and Napoleonic causation and pre-existing trends from acceleration; Haiti differs from client republics.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Mass warfare, state powers and reactive nationalism
findings.source_grounded_analysis: National mobilization made opponents expand conscription, policing and taxes. Anti-French fear outweighed resentment of domestic burdens. Sovereignty could be turned against France; Italy’s new nationalism differed from reinforced older patriotisms.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: mass warfare; Clausewitz; conscription; taxation; policing; nationalism; Italian nationalism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Treat Clausewitz passage as attributed analysis; avoid one-way diffusion or assuming French principles guaranteed French allegiance.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Popular endorsement became a durable criterion of legitimacy, often token or manipulated. Doyle distinguishes representative elections from street sovereignty and argues sansculotte excess may have delayed mass democracy despite inspiring later democrats.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: popular sovereignty; democracy; representation; plebiscites; political legitimacy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain ambiguity and author’s qualified retardation claim; do not substitute a simple triumph narrative.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Liberty: symbols, definitions and coercive practice
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Liberty imagery and classical republican symbols spread, but rulers used the term opportunistically. Rights-based non-harm, freedom from arbitrary power and freedoms of thought/worship remained ideals despite infringements and imposed French rule abroad.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: liberty; liberty trees; Phrygian caps; classical republicanism; Rights of Man
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish declared meaning, symbolic practice and coercive appropriation.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Rights/opportunity differed from equality of wealth or political access. Property remained protected and agrarian redistribution criminalized;1793 democratic constitution never operated. Fraternity appeared late and was soon dropped; later motto memory is retrospective.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: equality; property rights; political franchise; agrarian law; fraternity; Liberty Equality Fraternity
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep equality senses and chronology; no equivalence between legal equality and universal voting or economic redistribution.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Women acted in journées, religious resistance and informal influence; individual activists challenged roles. Male officials banned women’s organizations and rejected political equality, while Civil Code work narrowed property rights. Doyle qualifies some biographical assertions.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: women; October Days; women’s clubs; Claire Lacombe; Olympe de Gouges; Théroigne de Méricourt; nuns
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve women’s diverse political positions, male rationales as attributed, and uncertain espionage claim; not all female activity was feminist.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Right of resistance and invention of the revolutionary model
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Successive revolutionary regimes could not disown resistance principles grounding their own authority.1789 became a model, vocabulary and technique for consciously prepared later revolutions; Marxist and1989 examples show reach.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: right of resistance; insurrection; revolutionary identity; revolutionary models; Marxism; political symbolism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish Doyle’s claim of modern revolutionary novelty from a denial of all pre1789 uprisings.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Seating origins became ideological labels; revolutionary threat produced conscious conservative theories, especially Maistre’s religious/intransigent restoration. Moderate conservatives preferred reform; rigid repression could provoke renewed revolution.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Left and Right; conservatism; Maistre; Burke; Gentz; reform versus reaction
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Avoid treating all conservatism as identical or making a list of thinkers equivalent to identical detailed treatment.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Some social, state and economic trends might have continued without Revolution; specific anti-feudal ideology, religious rupture, popular democracy and mass warfare depended on contingencies. The ultimate judgment is profound cultural transformation and tragedy amid idealism and enormous human cost.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: revolutionary legacy; continuity/change; contingency; Enlightenment limits; cultural transformation; human cost
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve counterfactual modality and dual appraisal; not wholly futile, wholly progressive, or inevitable.
